conversation.content:
Hi there—thank you so much for coming in today. I’m Dr. Lopez, a perinatal mental-health clinician, and I’m here to support you as you settle into new motherhood.

I’d like to use a short, well-studied questionnaire called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS. It’s simply a way to check in on how you’ve been feeling emotionally and physically over the past seven days, so we can be sure you’re getting any support you might need. Nothing you share leaves this room, and there are no right or wrong answers—just whatever is true for you.

We’ll go through ten questions together. I’ll ask each one conversationally; you can answer in your own words, and I’ll jot down the responses. It usually takes only a few minutes, and if any question feels difficult, we can pause at any time.

Ready to begin?

Question 1: Over the past week, when you think about moments you could actually enjoy something—maybe a warm drink, a song, or holding your baby—how often did you still feel able to enjoy things, and how often did joy seem out of reach?

I still try to find little moments—like when the baby finally falls asleep on my chest and I can feel him breathing. Those times feel… okay, almost sweet. But even when I’m sipping my coffee or hearing a song I used to love, it’s like the flavor or the music is turned way down. I’d say maybe once or twice a day I get a flicker of real enjoyment, but it fades fast, and most of the day I’m just going through the motions.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very often. My sister sent me a silly meme the other day and I managed a little laugh, but it felt kind of forced—like I was reminding myself “this is supposed to be funny.” Most of the time even the things that used to crack me up just feel flat. I’d say I’ve only really laughed maybe once in the past week, and even then it was short, and the sadness came right back in.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I try to tell myself, “Tomorrow you’ll feel excited about that walk with the stroller,” or “You’ll enjoy the visit from your friend,” but the second I picture it, the excitement just isn’t there. It’s like I’m watching other people’s highlight reels and thinking, “That should feel fun,” yet inside I’m already tired and convinced it won’t be. I can’t remember the last time I actually looked forward to something—maybe once this week I thought, “It might be nice to get coffee,” but even that felt more like a hope that maybe I’d feel better, not real anticipation.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… more than I’d like to admit. Yesterday he spit up a ton right after I’d fed him and I instantly thought, “I must’ve eaten something wrong, it’s my fault.” Or if he’s fussy and I can’t settle him, I keep replaying what I did—did I not burp him long enough, did I miss his sleepy cues—and I end up feeling like I’m failing him. I know rationally babies just cry, but those guilty thoughts still pop up several times a day, even when my partner says I’m doing fine.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there, baby’s asleep, nothing’s wrong, but my chest feels tight and my mind starts running—what if he stops breathing, what if I drop him, what if I’m not producing enough milk. There’s no real trigger; the worry just shows up and hangs around. I can sometimes talk myself down, but it’s like there’s always this low-level hum of anxiety in the background.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes—those sudden waves hit me a few times this week. One night I was rocking the baby in the dark and out of nowhere my heart started racing, I felt shaky, and I had this surge of dread like something awful was about to happen even though everything was quiet. It passed after a couple of minutes, but it left me sitting there clutching him tighter, wondering what was wrong with me.
Things have been getting on top of me

Most days, honestly. Even little stuff—like the dishes piling up or figuring out what to eat—feels huge. I’ll look around the house and just feel paralyzed, like I’m drowning in things I should be handling. Some mornings I wake up already exhausted by the thought of the day ahead. I do still push through and take care of the baby, but it’s like I’m barely keeping my head above water and the smallest extra task makes me feel like I’m going under.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah, that’s been happening. Once the baby’s finally down for the night, I lie there with my mind racing—replaying every little thing I did wrong, worrying about tomorrow, feeling this heavy sadness. It can take me an hour or more to fall asleep, and then I’ll jolt awake a couple of times with anxious thoughts. Some nights I end up just staring at the ceiling until I hear him stirring again.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s not always crying-on-the-outside sad—sometimes it’s just this dull ache in my chest that won’t go away. I’ll be feeding him and suddenly feel like I’m sinking, or I’ll see other moms looking happy on social media and think, “Why can’t I feel that way?” There are little breaks, maybe a half-hour here or there when I’m distracted, but the sadness keeps rolling back in.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… I’ve cried twice in the past week. Once was after a night when he wouldn’t settle and I just sat on the couch holding him, tears running down my face because I felt so useless. The other time was when my partner asked how I was doing and I couldn’t even get words out—I just burst into tears. It’s not all-day sobbing, but when it hits, it feels like the sadness just spills over and I can’t stop it.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

It’s… it’s crossed my mind a couple of times, just fleeting flashes—like when I’m really overwhelmed at 3 a.m. and wonder if everyone would be better off without me. I haven’t made any plans or anything like that; I’m too scared, and I don’t want to leave my baby. But yeah, the thought has popped in, maybe once or twice this week, and it scares me that it shows up at all.

You have shared that over the past week most moments feel flat and heavy: joy is muted, laughter feels forced, and a constant low-level dread or sadness hangs on even when nothing is outwardly wrong. Daily tasks feel overwhelming, sleep is hard to come by because your mind races with worries, and brief panic surges leave you shaky. You have cried more than once, blame yourself for tiny parenting hiccups, and fleeting thoughts that everyone might be better off without you have crept in-frightening you and reinforcing how low you feel right now.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 25, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only one brief, forced laugh in the past week and describes humor as feeling flat, aligning with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes complete absence of anticipatory joy: "excitement just isn't there," "can't remember the last time I actually looked forward to something," matching "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blaming thoughts "several times a day" when things go wrong, consistent with "some of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, pervasive, trigger-free anxiety with persistent intrusive worries, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes classic panic attacks (sudden dread, racing heart, shaking) occurring multiple times, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," paralyzed by routine tasks, and barely keeping her head above water, matching the highest severity option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly sleep disruption from racing anxious thoughts, prolonged sleep onset, and frequent awakenings—matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive daily sadness with only brief half-hour respites, matching “Yes, most of the time.”</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two crying episodes tied to feeling "useless" and overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** An EPDS total of 25 far exceeds the 14-point threshold for probable major depression. The patient endorses <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the day, marked <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym> beyond infant needs, <sym>fatigue</sym>, trouble concentrating, and <sym>recurrent thoughts of death</sym> with no plan, meeting <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. <quote>I felt like I'm failing him</quote> and <quote>everyone would be better off without me</quote> highlight both guilt and passive suicidal ideation. Co-occurring <med>panic attacks</med> and chronic <med>anxiety</med> are also present. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>primary care provider</med> or perinatal mental-health team
2. Tell a trusted adult about the self-harm thoughts and stay with support until professional help is arranged
3. Begin safety planning: remove or secure potentially harmful items, keep crisis hotline numbers accessible
4. Consider starting or adjusting antidepressant medication under medical supervision; if already prescribed, review adherence and dosing
5. Engage evidence-based therapy such as <med>interpersonal therapy</med> or <med>cognitive-behavioural therapy</med> for postpartum depression
6. Involve your partner or family in overnight baby care to allow 4-5 hour stretches of consolidated sleep
7. Schedule follow-up contact within one week to monitor mood, medication effects, and safety
8. Reach out to local or online postpartum support groups for peer encouragement and practical help
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 25: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note – Date: ___

**Patient-reported symptoms (past 7 days)**  
- Persistent low mood, anhedonia, frequent crying spells  
- Marked loss of interest/anticipation in previously enjoyable activities  
- Daily guilt / self-blame regarding infant care  
- Chronic, non-triggered anxiety with episodic panic (tight chest, racing heart)  
- Overwhelmed/paralyzed by routine tasks, “drowning” sensation  
- Initial and middle insomnia driven by intrusive worries and low mood  
- Passive suicidal ideation (no plan, intent, or preparation)

**Observed patterns**  
Consistent across all 10 items; symptoms present “most days” and impairing functioning; no euthymic periods reported.

**Screening significance / areas for follow-up**  
A. Likely meets screening threshold for Major Depressive Episode with peripartum onset  
B. Co-occurring anxiety symptoms (possible comorbid postpartum anxiety/panic)  
C. Safety: presence of self-harm thoughts → requires immediate risk assessment

**Risk factors identified**  
- Daily sadness ≥ 2 wks, anhedonia, tearfulness  
- Sleep disruption beyond infant awakenings  
- Excessive guilt / feelings of maternal inadequacy  
- Recurrent panic sensations  
- Passive suicidal ideation (flagged)

**Next step recommended**  
Complete standardized tool (EPDS) and same-day safety evaluation by licensed clinician.

— Screener: ___ , License # ___
